body:
Why plants need nutrients

Crop plants require water, sunlight, air and essential nutrients for normal growth, development and reproduction. Green plants manufacture carbohydrates through photosynthesis, using carbon dioxide and water in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll. However, carbohydrates alone cannot provide all the substances needed to build plant cells, proteins and other compounds.

Plants also require mineral nutrients. Roots absorb many of these nutrients from the soil, mainly in dissolved forms. Farmers add fertilisers or manure when the available nutrient supply is insufficient for the crop's requirements.

Soil fertility is the capacity of soil to supply essential plant nutrients in adequate amounts and suitable proportions for plant growth. It is an important component of overall soil productivity, which also depends on water, soil structure and other conditions.

Essential nutrients and their classification

Plant nutrients are classified as macronutrients and micronutrients according to the amounts plants require. This classification does not indicate that micronutrients are less essential.

Macronutrients

Macronutrients are required in relatively large quantities. Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen are obtained mainly from air and water. The principal mineral macronutrients include nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, calcium, magnesium and sulphur.

Among these, nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and potassium (K) are called the primary fertiliser nutrients because they commonly require substantial replenishment in agricultural soils. Calcium, magnesium and sulphur are generally called secondary nutrients.

Micronutrients

Micronutrients are required in small quantities but remain essential for normal plant functioning. Examples include iron, zinc, manganese, copper, boron, molybdenum, chlorine and nickel. A shortage of even one essential micronutrient can restrict crop growth despite an adequate NPK supply.

The distinct functions of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium

NutrientImportant functionsBroad deficiency effects
Nitrogen (N)Formation of proteins, chlorophyll and nucleic acids; vegetative growthReduced growth and yellowing, often first noticeable in older leaves
Phosphorus (P)Energy transfer, root development, cell formation and reproductive growthStunted growth, weak root development and delayed maturity
Potassium (K)Regulation of water balance, enzyme activity and stomatal functioningReduced stress tolerance and leaf-edge damage in some crops

These are broad patterns, not conclusive diagnoses. Similar symptoms can result from water stress, diseases or other nutrient disorders. Soil testing and crop assessment are therefore important before selecting a fertiliser.

Why continuous cultivation can reduce soil fertility

When a crop is harvested, nutrients contained in its grains, stems and other harvested parts are removed from the field. Rainfall and irrigation may also carry some soluble nutrients beyond the root zone. Continuous cultivation without adequate nutrient replenishment can gradually reduce soil fertility.

Fertilisers replace particular nutrients, while organic manure contributes nutrients and organic matter. Biological processes, including microbial nitrogen fixation and decomposition, also help maintain nutrient cycling.

Fertilisers are not plant food in the same sense as carbohydrates. Plants make carbohydrates through photosynthesis. Fertilisers supply mineral nutrients needed for growth and the synthesis of many plant substances.

Prelims focus

  • N, P and K are the primary fertiliser nutrients.
  • Calcium, magnesium and sulphur are secondary macronutrients.
  • Iron, zinc and boron are examples of micronutrients.
  • Nitrogen is important for chlorophyll and protein formation.
  • Phosphorus is associated with energy transfer and root development.
  • Trap: Micronutrients are required in smaller quantities; they are not optional nutrients.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 7, Chapter 1, Nutrition in Plants, pp. 1–4, 2018–19 reprint; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 15, Improvement in Food Resources, section 15.1.2(i), Nutrient Management, pp. 205–207, 2018–19 reprint.]

title: Plant Nutrients, Soil Fertility and the Importance of NPK

body:
What is a fertiliser?

A fertiliser is a material applied to soil or plants to supply nutrients needed for growth. Fertilisers may be mineral, organic or specially formulated products. In school-level agricultural science, the term chemical fertiliser commonly refers to manufactured products containing one or more plant nutrients in concentrated and relatively predictable amounts.

Examples include urea, diammonium phosphate, superphosphate, potassium chloride and NPK fertilisers.

Classification according to the nutrients supplied

Single-primary-nutrient or straight fertilisers

A straight fertiliser principally supplies one primary nutrient: nitrogen, phosphorus or potassium. It may also contain a secondary nutrient.

  • Urea: A concentrated nitrogenous fertiliser containing approximately 46% nitrogen by mass. Its chemical formula is CO(NH2)2.
  • Single superphosphate (SSP): A phosphatic fertiliser that also supplies sulphur and calcium.
  • Muriate of potash (MOP): Potassium chloride, a major source of potassium for crops.
  • Ammonium sulphate: A nitrogenous fertiliser that also supplies sulphur.

The presence of a secondary nutrient does not automatically make a fertiliser a multi-primary-nutrient product. For example, ammonium sulphate supplies nitrogen and sulphur but not phosphorus and potassium.

Complex and mixed fertilisers

Complex or compound fertilisers contain more than one primary plant nutrient as part of a manufactured fertiliser product. Mixed fertilisers are produced by physically blending fertiliser materials to obtain a desired nutrient composition. Both can supply multiple primary nutrients, but their manufacturing characteristics differ.

Diammonium phosphate (DAP) is an important NP fertiliser because it supplies both nitrogen and phosphorus. NPK fertilisers contain nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium in stated proportions.

Understanding the NPK grade

A conventional fertiliser grade such as 18-46-0 expresses the percentage by mass of nitrogen (N), phosphorus reported as phosphorus pentoxide equivalent (P2O5) and potassium reported as potassium oxide equivalent (K2O), respectively.

FertiliserTypical gradeMain nutrient distinction
Urea46-0-0Nitrogen source
DAP18-46-0Nitrogen and phosphorus source
NPK fertiliser12-32-16Contains all 3 primary nutrients

For ordinary DAP, 18-46-0 means 18% nitrogen, 46% P2O5 equivalent and no declared potassium. The second number is not the percentage of elemental phosphorus. Similarly, the third number expresses K2O equivalent, not elemental potassium.

DAP does not supply all 3 primary nutrients. It provides nitrogen and phosphorus but does not provide potassium as a declared primary nutrient. A crop requiring additional potassium may need a separate potassium source.

Fertilisers and manures are not the same

Manure is organic material derived from decomposed plant or animal matter. It usually contains nutrients at lower concentrations than common mineral fertilisers, but it also contributes organic matter that improves soil structure and water-holding capacity.

CharacteristicMineral fertiliserOrganic manure
Typical sourceManufactured mineral or chemical materialsPlant and animal residues
Nutrient concentrationOften relatively high and specifiedUsually lower and more variable
Organic matterGenerally little or noneContributes organic matter
Additional soil benefitCorrects particular nutrient shortagesImproves soil structure and water retention

Important types of manure

  • Farmyard manure: Decomposed cattle dung, urine-soaked litter and related farm residues.
  • Compost: Organic material produced through decomposition of plant and animal wastes.
  • Vermicompost: Compost produced with the assistance of earthworms.
  • Green manure: Green plants, such as sunn hemp or dhaincha, grown and incorporated into soil to contribute organic matter and nutrients.

Leguminous green-manure crops may also support biological nitrogen fixation through their association with nitrogen-fixing bacteria.

Other ways to classify fertilisers

Fertilisers can also be classified by their physical form, such as granules, powders, water-soluble products and liquids. Nano fertilisers are a specialised formulation category involving nanoscale particles or structures.

These classifications answer different questions. A fertiliser may simultaneously be nitrogenous, manufactured and liquid. Its physical form does not determine which nutrients it contains.

Prelims focus

  • Urea is a concentrated nitrogenous fertiliser containing approximately 46% nitrogen.
  • DAP is an NP fertiliser with the conventional grade 18-46-0.
  • The conventional NPK grade expresses N, P2O5 equivalent and K2O equivalent.
  • Vermicompost involves earthworms; green manure involves incorporation of green plant material.
  • Mineral fertilisers supply nutrients, while organic manures also add organic matter.
  • Trap: The 46 in DAP 18-46-0 does not mean 46% elemental phosphorus.

[Sources: NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 1, Crop Production and Management, section 1.5, Adding Manure and Fertilisers, pp. 5–7, 2018–19 reprint; NCERT, Science, Class 9, Chapter 15, Improvement in Food Resources, section 15.1.2(i), pp. 206–207, 2018–19 reprint; IFFCO, DAP 18-46-0, product description and application section, consulted 3 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Three independent criteria classify fertilisers; nano urea is nitrogenous, manufactured, and a liquid nano formulation.
pictures.caption: A fertiliser can be classified independently by nutrient content, origin and physical form.

title: Types of Fertilisers, Nutrient Grades and Organic Manures

body:
What makes a fertiliser a nano fertiliser?

Nanotechnology deals with materials or structures at extremely small dimensions. A nanometre (nm) is one-billionth of a metre. At this scale, the size and surface characteristics of particles can influence how they disperse, interact with surfaces and release their contents.

A nano fertiliser is a nutrient-supplying formulation that uses nanoscale particles or structures to deliver plant nutrients. The term describes a feature of the formulation, not a separate essential plant nutrient.

IFFCO describes nitrogen-containing particles of approximately 20–50 nm in its nano urea technology. Its Nano DAP liquid product description identifies particles smaller than 100 nm. These are product-specific descriptions; not every nano fertiliser has the same particle size or composition.

How plant nutrients reach crops

Root uptake from soil

Most conventional fertilisers are applied to the soil. Their nutrients dissolve or undergo chemical transformations and become available for absorption through roots. This is especially important early in crop growth, when roots are establishing and the plant requires a reliable nutrient supply.

A fertiliser applied before sowing or at sowing is commonly called a basal application. Later applications to a standing crop are called top-dressing or supplementary applications, depending on the method used.

Foliar application through leaves

Foliar application means applying a suitable nutrient solution to the leaves of a standing crop. Some nutrients can be taken up through leaf surfaces, so foliar feeding may supplement soil nutrition.

Foliar uptake depends on the formulation, crop, leaf characteristics, weather and application conditions. It does not mean that every sprayed particle automatically enters a plant or that roots become unnecessary.

Seed treatment

Some fertiliser formulations, including specified nano DAP products, can be applied as a seed treatment according to their authorised directions. The purpose is to make selected nutrients available during the early stages of crop development.

Seed treatment, soil application and foliar spraying are different methods. A method suitable for one product should not automatically be used for another.

Why nano formulations are being developed

Conventional nutrient applications are not always fully utilised by crops. Some nutrients may be lost through leaching, runoff, volatilisation or other soil processes. Nanoscale formulations are being investigated and promoted because their properties may help improve nutrient delivery and utilisation in certain situations.

Nutrient-use efficiency describes how effectively supplied nutrients contribute to plant growth and production. An improvement in nutrient-use efficiency can sometimes allow a crop to achieve a satisfactory yield with a smaller quantity of a particular fertiliser.

However, nutrient-use efficiency and total nutrient supply are not the same thing. A highly efficient nitrogen formulation still supplies nitrogen, not phosphorus or potassium.

What nano fertilisers cannot automatically do

  • They cannot correct a deficiency of an essential nutrient that the formulation does not contain.
  • They cannot replace adequate water, suitable soil conditions or appropriate crop management.
  • They do not automatically eliminate the need for basal fertilisation.
  • They do not guarantee identical crop responses across all soils, crops and seasons.

In a statement-based question, the strongest distinction is between potentially improved delivery and guaranteed complete replacement. The first can be scientifically reasonable; the second requires evidence and specific conditions.

Prelims focus

  • 1 nm equals one-billionth of a metre.
  • IFFCO describes nano urea particles of approximately 20–50 nm.
  • IFFCO describes its Nano DAP liquid particles as smaller than 100 nm.
  • Foliar application targets leaves; basal fertilisation supplies nutrients through the soil.
  • A nano fertiliser is not necessarily a biofertiliser.
  • Trap: Small particle size alone does not establish that a product can fully replace conventional fertilisation.

[Sources: IFFCO, Nano Urea Plus (Liquid), product description, and Nano DAP (Liquid), product description, both consulted 3 November 2026; Department of Fertilisers, Press Information Bureau, Government Highlights Significant Progress in Nano-Fertilizer Adoption and Drone-Led Agricultural Transformation, 20 March 2026, release 2242958, consulted 3 November 2026.]

title: Nano Fertilisers: Meaning, Nutrient Delivery and Application
